utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. May I remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, can I just remind you where we had ended last night. You had been to the Velepromet facility, certain people had left you, you had then ensured that the buses were loaded at that time. And do you remember giving your evidence about that, in very general terms. Not that you gave the evidence in general terms, but that you remember that that was what was being said. Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with then with the buses went, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lingered for a while in the compound with the officers who were still there, Branko Korica, Second Lieutenant Cekic and his junior officers. At this point in time I managed to notice that Vojvoda Topola was back within the compound. As far as I was able to see, he had had a change of clothes. He had a new camouflage uniform on and he was with a woman who was approximately as tall as he was. It seemed to me as if he was there to show off and let me know clearly what he thought of me. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you what he thought of you? Did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't speak to me. He was with his Chetniks, and he just walked by for us to see him, after which he returned with this lady. After that he left the Velepromet compound altogether and left the compound, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were loading the buses, or indeed prior to loading the buses, did you hear any shooting nearby?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were loading people on to buses the buses were already facing the gate and the exit. The order had been given that the buses would leave the compound and park in line along the road. The buses were then being taken over by an officer from the military police. I didn't know this officer, but the column formed was his responsibility. While the buses were still inside the compound before leaving and I had not yet issued my command, I was warned by Warrant Officer Korica that the Chetniks and the TO people were taking people away. The officers and the police officers were taking people to board the buses and at the same time the Chetniks and the TO people were taking them somewhere outside the compound where they could no longer be seen, and then bursts of gun-fire were subsequently heard. As I have already pointed out, Korica then went on to warn me about the fact that Marko Crevar had been overheard as saying that, "This colonel, too, should be killed along with the Ustashas." At this point in time -- or, rather, after some Colonel Janovic [as interpreted] came to see me and he confirmed these threats. He said he had heard them, too, and also said that the Chetniks were taking prisoners of war somewhere outside and that shots could be heard. I was told the same thing by Stosic later on, Slobodan Stosic. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, perhaps my apologies. But I just want to deal with one or two other matters before we proceed. When we're talking about the number of being taken away on the buses, or being evacuated on the buses, would you be able to give an indication of how many people actually were evacuated from the Velepromet facility that evening?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to be specific. I can't really give you a specific answer. However, I did learn something about the number of people by counting the buses on their way out. My conclusion at the time was that we had managed to evacuate about 800 POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Obviously you left Velepromet. Where did you then go after Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was much affected by everything that had gone on. I was much affected by what I had experienced at the hands of Vojvoda Topola, as well as some of my own colleagues, such as Tomic and Kijanovic. I headed back to the command post accompanied by some military police officers. The distance between Velepromet and the command post being about five kilometres because that's what I think it was at the time, we walked as soldiers do, and if the calculation is that if you do the military step you make 60 steps a minute. I think it might have taken us between 30 and 45 minutes to eventually get there. That evening Tomic, Major Sljivancanin and some other people were at the command post. I was bitter and angry. I tried to approach Colonel Mrksic to tell him about what had been going on. At one point in time there was an opportunity and I seized it. I walked up to him, and as far as I can now remember I said, "Commander, do you have any idea what was going on over there? People killed. This is an attack against the integrity of the JNA. This is an attack against you as a commander. This is an attack against all of us. There was a Chetnik duke, as they called him, who wanted to slit my throat in front of all the Ustashas on that bus. That is a disgrace." I saluted him and walked right out of the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you told Colonel Mrksic that people were being killed, did he say anything to you about that? Did he reply?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Mrksic was silent. He heard me out, but he remained silent and replied nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Major Sljivancanin hear you telling Colonel Mrksic that people were being killed at the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that anyone had heard, neither can I remember who exactly was there, but there were quite a number of people present. I remember that General Jerko Crmaric appeared, accompanied by some of his colonels. He was from the logistics body of the 1st Military District. I shared with him as well what I had experienced at Velepromet. He heard my story but said that he was here on a mission given to him by the logistics security and because of the evacuation, so he did not really reply to my story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say that you told General Jerko your story, did that include the fact that killings had been going on in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no such information available at the time. I did not know whether the Chetniks or the TO had held anyone back there. It was a huge area, and it was night-time. There was no lighting, no considerable lighting except the lighting that was there within the compound. It's also a rather large area and it would have been possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Pardon me, I just interrupt a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One correction to make in the transcript. When the Prosecutor asked about General Jerko Crmaric, he said he was there as logistical back-up, but we see on page 4 of the transcript, line 19, that -- line 21 and 22, that -- that he heard this on a mission given to him by the logistics security. We have the word "hear," h-e-a-r, instead of "here," h-e-r-e, if that could please be clarified. I think that is a substantial matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm considered about, the were difficulties yesterday about - and I don't criticise in anyway - translation and also the electronics. I have asked a question - I don't know if the witness can hear this or not, I hope he can't - but the answer that is given is completely inconsistent with the evidence that he's given some time before. And that does -- that is something that would cause me concern. So I would like to re-ask the question, if I may, because it is really quite a perverse answer in some ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Moore, if you see problems of that nature, go over the same ground again without seeking leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, can you just listen, please, very carefully to my question. If you have having difficulties in understanding or hearing, please say so. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I follow you. It's loud and clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have told this Court that you told Colonel Mrksic that killings had been occurring at Velepromet and he made no reply and you then left. Now, that's right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with Major Sljivancanin. Did you mention to Sljivancanin either directly at that time or subsequently about what you had found at Velepromet? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, this question was asked on line 14. And the witness provided a crystal clear answer on line 16. "[In English] ... anyone had heard, neither can I remember who exactly was there, but there were quite a number of people ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Lukic, but there are some apparent difficulties in what is appearing. They may not be difficulties; that is being confirmed at the moment. If there are difficulties, it's not clear whether it's with an understanding of the question or whether it's in the interpretation and translation or where it is. But on this occasion I have just indicated to Mr. Moore he may do this thing, unusually. If there is no problem with the answer, it will be the same answer comes again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. The problem may be that I was listening to the witness in my own language, and I wasn't really focusing on the transcript. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's often a problem, Mr. Lukic. Really the Bench is irrelevant in these proceedings, but it doesn't hurt to listen to us occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I ask it this in way, which I hope will not impinge on anybody's sensibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that you told Mrksic about the killings at Velepromet. Who else did you tell at Negoslavci that there was killing at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Slavko Tomic, having left the command post, said that Major Sljivancanin would hold a brief meeting in order to brief us on the conclusions regarding the mission that had been accomplished and in order to give us a brief outline of the task to be carried out on the 20th of November, which was the evacuation of the hospital. As far as I remember, the meeting was to be held in an area outside the command post. This had already been the case when we had received our tasks about Velepromet. Major Sljivancanin provided the briefest possible outline of the fact that the mission had been accomplished as far as Velepromet was concerned. Slavko Tomic immediately came up with a number of questions. I interrupted by saying, "Killings occurred there, killings were committed there. You have no idea what I saw there, what I experienced there. The Chetniks were about to slit my throat, and you left me behind." Slavko Tomic again said, "Mission completed." Major Sljivancanin merely confirmed that the mission had indeed been completed, that the buses had been seen off and sent on their way to Sremska Mitrovica. And as far as I remember, he also said that the buses holding women, refugees from Vukovar and other civilians, such as the elderly and children, had been sent to the Croatian border somewhere. As far as I remember, it was said that there had been several attempts -- well, actually those Croatian citizens, there were several attempts to send them back to the Croatian authorities, but that they were sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just, before we proceed any further, go back to what you've told us. You said that you had interrupted and told the meeting that killings occurred there and that there were killings there. "You have no idea what I saw there, what I experienced there." Did Major Sljivancanin say anything to you about those killings at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Major Sljivancanin did not say anything to me about it, except for saying that the mission was completed. I do apologise, I have to point out that I mentioned Colonel Kijanovic too. I told you that you had informed me about the fact that he had heard about killings and that there were bodies there. That same evening, at that same meeting, and I'm positive that it was also at the next meeting, on the 20th of November, the morning of the 20th of November, the meeting held by Major Sljivancanin at the Velepromet gate, when he briefed us on the elements of the -- of our next task, the evacuation of the hospital. I'll be telling you more about this later on. However, it's essential that I pointed out that Colonel Kijanovic briefed me, said that he knew and that Korica, too, knew that there had been killings over there and that there were dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, what I want it try and do, so that I can explain, I want to try and give my evidence, or the questions so that we deal with evidence in compartments. So we'll deal with the meeting, move on to an additional meeting. We'll try and break it into segments, if we can, as we're getting very long answers now. So I just want to deal, if I may, with this piece of evidence that you've given about Colonel Kijanovic telling you about dead bodies. I'm going to break the sequence of time for a moment. Do you know if in actual fact there was any attempt to find those dead bodies? Now, do you understand the question or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, and my answer is that I am not aware whether before the meeting somebody had taken any measures to find those bodies, although I don't think that they did, because it was night-time, and it would have been difficult to search the area and find the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what about in the morning, do you know if there was -- or the next day, was there any attempt to find bodies the next day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to talk about the substance of the meeting later on. In response to your question I asked Colonel Kijanovic to address the superiors, the commanding officers, of the unit of Colonel Mrksic to search both within and without the compound of Velepromet to uncover dead bodies, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know if that was done?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we met that day outside the command post, that's to say on the 20th in the evening at about 7.00 p.m., Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There may be a translation error in relation to p.m. Is it 7.00 in the morning or 7.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it was at 7.00 p.m.; that's to say, at 7.00 in the evening. I apologise. Perhaps I misspoke or did not speak in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you continue then, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by Colonels Tomic and Kijanovic that the buses left the Velepromet compound for Ovcara, and Colonel Kijanovic told me that while I was on my way with Major Sljivancanin to the hospital he, together with a group of senior officers from Colonel Mrksic's unit and military police, searched the premises and found 17 corpses, that these dead bodies were transported on a military truck that was in the possession of Colonel Mrksic's unit. I asked him where were they taken, and he told me that they were taken to the military cemetery and that they were buried there. Then I asked him where the military cemetery was and whether they had taken any measures to identify the bodies and whether any forensic officers were involved in examining the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you get an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Colonel Kijanovic, as I said, found that -- that 17 dead bodies had been found and that they were taken on a military truck to the military cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the question came out of a -- an answer that was perhaps misinterpreted. That's page 10, line 14. He did not ask Kijanovic, as far as I understood, whether the forensics were involved and whether these bodies were examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is no guarantee of accuracy, is that he had. That was the interpretation that -- that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I believe, was querying the interpretation. Is that right? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I am entirely sympathetic if there is errors on translation, but it is very unfair on a witness who is focusing on an account and there is consistency of interruption, I don't criticise the interruption, but it is a very destabilising process for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a difficult issue, Mr. Moore. We have generally been assisted by those who have identified errors in the -- what appears in the translation or on the transcript. It is a process that can be abused; I am well aware of that. If that should occur, we would certainly put an end to it. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sorry for pulling you, as it were, off a topic for a -- about the meeting. I would like to return to the meeting that you had had with Tomic and Sljivancanin when you returned. When that meeting ended, were there any arrangements made to meet on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have understood you well, your question refers to the meeting that was also held on the 20th outside the command post, which means that the meeting could have been held at around 1.00 or -- 0200 or 0100 on the 20th, and I can repeat what Major Sljivancanin stated there, if necessary. If I've understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you in very general terms tell us what Major Sljivancanin said, and we'll take it from there.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin talked about the mission, the forthcoming mission on the evacuation of the hospital. He told us that he had received lists from Dr. Vesna Bosanac. I can't remember whether he indicated if this was a unified, compiled list comprising the lists drafted by Dr. Njavro and Marin Bili, but I understood him to mean that the list covered the hospital staff, the wounded, and the sick, including the ones that were called criminals, the ones who were hiding there. I understood him to mean that all these persons were on the list. That was how Major Sljivancanin came by the -- this very important information, which would facilitate the process of evacuation of the hospital. Major Sljivancanin said that the hospital was to be vacated according to an evacuation plan, that he would personally be in charge of this mission, that not all of us would be able to go over there. Rather, we would gather at 0600 hours at the gate of Velepromet on the 20th in the morning. If you have understood me, I told you now that there were two meetings where Major Sljivancanin addressed the tasks relating to the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you've told us that there was going to be a meeting at 0600 hours outside the gates of the Velepromet facility, the same facility you had been to. Did you actually attend the meeting at 6.00 in the morning, 0600, as requested?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We gathered at 0600 hours at the gate to Velepromet inside the compound, outside the administrative building there. I cannot tell you specifically who was first to arrive there, but I remember that we were among the first ones there. There were Colonel Slavko Tomic, myself, Kijanovic, Slobodan Stosic, Stevan Mirkovic. And that there were senior officers below Major Muncan, Dragan, that there was Korica there, as well as some other officers. Major Sljivancanin arrived in -- in a military all-terrain vehicle, together with his escorts. There was another officer, a captain there with him, and I believe the vehicle was driven by a junior officer. The meeting was quite brief, and as far as I remember, Major Sljivancanin said that everything was to go to plan, as he had informed us earlier, that only one senior officer from among those of us who were present there could accompany him over to the hospital, because he did not have any extra seats in the vehicle. We looked at each other, and I don't know if somebody suggested that I go or how it happened, but it was stated that I should inspect the hospital from the perspective of the application of international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal with two issues. Firstly, when you were at the Velepromet gate, did you see any other vehicle parked there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that there was an all-terrain vehicle parked there with foreign registration plates, but I didn't know whether it belonged to Medecins sans Frontieres or to representatives of the International Red Cross. The window-panes were fogged over and frozen. I was unable to see whether there was anybody seated in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What colour was the vehicle; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicle was grey in colour -- oh, no, it was white, and it bore the sign of the International Red Cross, I think. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but that's the impression I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter that I wish to deal with was that you stated that you were going to inspect the hospital in respect of the international laws of war. Now, did you then go to the hospital from the Velepromet facility? Can you just answer yes or no on that, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how did you get there? What method of transport?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got there in Major Sljivancanin's vehicle. I believe it is relevant for me to state that he agreed that I should accompany him. However, I told him at the time that I wanted Warrant Officer Korica to accompany me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we go on to deal with that issue, you went in Sljivancanin's vehicle to the hospital from Velepromet. Did you have any difficulties driving on the roads to the hospital? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we did have any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we deal with -- you said that you wanted Warrant Officer Korica to accompany you to the hospital. Why did you want that? Why did you want that officer to accompany you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained my request to him. I told him, "You know what I experienced yesterday at the Velepromet and that my life was still at -- is still at risk because I was threatened from more than one quarters." And that's when Major Sljivancanin agreed and Warrant Officer Korica accompanied me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal now, please, with your arrival at the hospital. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you any idea, approximately, when you arrived at the hospital itself? You have a meeting at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have the image of those events back then fresh in my mind. We were going down toward the centre of Vukovar when darkness started setting in when you can see only the outlines of the building when one cannot discern the details. When we passed by the marketplace we were going down the street, I was surprised to see the town destroyed. It looked like a ghost town, buildings without any roofs on, and many of them are wrecked. I said out loud, "Well, Vukovar is a ghost town." Nobody responded to that. When we came down the main street, I recall seeing civilians approaching Major Sljivancanin's vehicle asking where they could find the army, because they wanted to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that I asked you was: Have you any idea what time you arrived at the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we got there at around 0700 hours, roughly speaking. May have been 7.15 or perhaps 7.30. But that's how I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you got to the hospital, were you able to see whether the hospital was being guarded by any units?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that there were military police guarding the hospital and they were under Major Sljivancanin's command. I also observed the presence of members of the Territorial Defence there who were wearing a sort of a national folk costume, but they carried military weapons and had bits and pieces of military gear. However, on their heads they wore this folk cap which is a red type of cap, and it may have had a patch or some insignia as well, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have heard evidence about a meeting in the Vukovar Hospital that morning. Were you aware of a meeting being held that morning in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Major Sljivancanin proceeded to act in accordance with his plan. If -- whether there was an officer there reporting to him somewhere, that's something I did not witness. I was touring the building and trying to see what the situation was like. As I entered one room, I saw that Major Sljivancanin had gathered all the hospital staff that was present there in one room. It was actually to the right from the emergency ward.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, to the left of the emergency ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you present when the meeting was taking place or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present at the meeting because I was unable to enter the room. However, I was there and I was able to follow what was going on. I could see the hospital staff arrive there. I stood next to a nurse who was obviously on duty that night in the -- in the nuclear shelter where the wounded were placed for their safety, and I talked to her, put a question or two to her, and I was following as Major Sljivancanin was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you go around the hospital at all that morning?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this brief meeting that Major Sljivancanin held with the hospital staff, he told him [as interpreted] the basic information that the hospital was to be vacated, that they could choose how they wished to be evacuated; I believe he gave them three options. As he went out, the hospital staff went to get their belongings and went out to wait for the buses and the International Red Cross, depending on which option they decided for. I asked Major Sljivancanin to pick out one medical doctor who was very familiar with the hospital and to allow him to accompany me, and I asked him also to assign two soldiers who would also -- to serve as escorts while we toured the hospital. Then he introduced me to the commander of the military police there - I can't remember what his last name was; he told me his last name - and he brought over a lance-corporal and two police officers. Major Sljivancanin said that Dr. Stanojevic should accompany me. He was -- he was specialised in internal medicine, and he was a member of the board and the head of the internal department, and he was the one -- of the internal ward, and he was the one who showed me the hospital. Warrant Officer Korica was also there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How long did you tour the hospital for internally?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our tour of the hospital started at 8.00 and lasted until 11.00. We toured the hospital following a certain order. First of all, we wanted to see where the nuclear shelter was, where the wounded had taken cover. Since Major Sljivancanin had said that the ones who would be -- that the first ones to leave the hospital would be the -- those who were able to walk, including the wounded, this was the way it was, in fact, done. They started leaving the hospital out the main entrance or exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you inspect the roof? I'm not suggesting you climbed on the roof, but did you inspect the roof itself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I came to the attic area, this is what they referred to as the attic area, since there was no roof left. This area was covered with roof-tiles. I don't know if I was clear enough when I say roof-tiles. They had wooden beams and roof-tiles atop. I remember seeing a large hole on these roof-tiles, and Dr. Stanojevic said that this had been caused by a plane bomb, which pierced through two levels of the building and landed in a corridor above the nuclear shelter where there were a number of wounded persons lying on stretchers or hospital beds. One of the wounded persons had his legs up in the air, both legs plastered, and the bomb went through his legs without hurting him. However, he got so scared that he fainted. I asked then what happened to the bomb. He said that policemen had arrived and specialists from the MUP. They inspected the bomb and took it to the police administration headed by Stipe Pole, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to deal again with the hospital. I think it's right that there was a bad smell in the hospital; is that correct? The English word is "stench."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember experiencing this, or rather all of us experienced this when we came to this huge refrigerator, the doors of which were open. And we could see body organs inside the refrigerators. Human body organs. I asked Dr. Stanojevic, "Where is this stench coming from?" As a soldier, I was able to withstand something like that, something that unpleasant, and I came closer to inspect what it was all about. Stanojevic said that those were human body organs and that in accordance with the law and medical regulation, certain organs have to be buried using the same procedure as a human corpse, whereas some other body parts have to be burned. Since they were out of electricity for quite a long time, the refrigerator wasn't functioning, started defrosting, and the body parts inside started perishing and became too -- caused the stench. I apologise, I also have to add that he said that a commission was in charge of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, if we deal with the inspection of the hospital, I think it's right to say that you found some bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside of the hospital compound we found corpses lined up bearing numbers. We saw that corpses had been registered or recorded. Dr. Stanojevic said that the coroner kept accurate records of the dead and that he believed that the book had been handed over to Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The doctor that you're referring to, Dr. Stanojevic, as I think you have called him, did he give any indication of the sort of missile or weapons that had been used in the hospital environment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a leading question. We didn't even hear that this had been used, and my learned friend is asking what sort of missile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will rephrase it if it helps. I was really trying to use a generic term as opposed to anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I must say Mr. Vasic, I see nothing erroneous in what was put. It was directing the doctor [sic] to a specific and different and new area of conversation. The choice of language was one that was merely searching for an answer which identified types of explosives, and I don't think carried the implication that you saw in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to answer that question? Would you like me to ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You had a doctor with you who obviously knew around about the hospital. Did he indicate to you the sort of weapon --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Did he indicate to you what sort of weapons had been used on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctor was more knowledgeable about medical issues. However, he showed me some things, and he said that after that bomb measures had been taken to move the wounded from the first level down below to the nuclear shelter where the living and working conditions were difficult, but this was the decision taken by the hospital Crisis Staff. In addition, he said that a lot of missiles or mortar shells had been fired into the compound of the hospital, mortar or some other pieces, but that he wasn't aware whether anybody had been hurt or killed. Also, he said that a shell had been fired on the part of the hospital which was above the emergency ward and had a covered veranda, and this was sort of an outer area of that building that was protruding from the building. I was able to see the hole made by this shell and could tell that this was a large calibre shell. But I didn't see any other major damage except for the structural damage, and I could see that it produced a psychological effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were going around the hospital, did you find any weapons there inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the attic of the hospital I found traces of what we would call evidence suggesting that there was military activity, or an activity taken by a military unit or, rather, that this was used as a look-out area. I asked whether this was a MUP unit or a unit of the National Guards Corps, and Dr. Stanojevic told me that there had been a squad of the National Guards Corps protecting the hospital. I asked him who was the commander of that unit, and he said that the commander was nicknamed Veliki Bojler. He was a large man, and -- and his appearance was intimidating. And apparently, based on what he heard, this is the affect he had on civilians and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that I asked you was: Did you find any weapons in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I should have answered specifically your question at the outset. I didn't find any weapons. I found traces, and I found the room in which the ZNG members were. I also found two flack jackets, which I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted you. You found two flack jackets, and I think you handed them over; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two flack jackets of NATO issue, and one belt for ammunition for a hunting rifle. I thought it belonged to -- or, rather, I thought that it came with an automatic hunting rifle and that it belonged to the MUP organ. I think that there were weapons at the hospital because I inspected the hospital in view of this, and naturally the soldiers, members of the unit, be it of MUP or ZNG, who had been wounded and brought in from their positions would be brought in with their weapons. I can't remember who told me this, but I heard that these weapons were later stored in an organised fashion within a room in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we deal, please, with the arrival of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the ICRC. Do you remember the ICRC arriving?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only twice before I started touring the hospital that I went outside. In my statement you can probably see that I said that one of the TO members wearing this tasselled cap brought to me a man, rather short, from the hospital, from the atomic shelter, and said to me, "Colonel, this is a war criminal." And then he mentioned his nickname, Joja or Jajo, something like that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, I think there may be some problem. I asked the question again, I'm quite sure you will be asked about that. But I would like to ask about the Red Cross? Do you understand? Thank you very much. Now, do you remember the Red Cross arriving at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from Branko Korica. He went away from me several times, descended down and went outside of the compound, most likely in order to see what was going on. When we made arrangements concerning the return to Velepromet, then he said -- or rather, I noticed that on the lawn in front of the hospital there was Dr. Ivezic, new chief of the hospital, and a JNA colonel, rather lieutenant-colonel. I saw him talking to a person in white overalls who I thought was a representative of the International Red Cross. It was then that I asked Korica who that was. And he said to me, This is a member of the International Red Cross or perhaps Medecins sans Frontieres with whom Major Sljivancanin had a verbal clash. I was surprised to hear that and I asked him where this had happened, and he said somewhere there in front of the hospital or at the hospital entrance. I didn't ask him about the details any further. Then -- I apologise. Then I approached Dr. -- Lieutenant-colonel Ivezic and the ICRC representative. If you wish me to explain further, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I think that won't be necessary. Thank you very much. It may be that you will be asked some questions about that; I know not. During your time at the hospital, who was in charge of the evacuation of the people from the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting on two occasions Major Sljivancanin explained to all of us that there was a special plan for evacuation of the hospital and that he personally would be in charge of the implementation of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you remember leaving the hospital that morning?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, that morning. You mean arrival or what? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've already arrived at the hospital, and I'm going to ask you -- I think it's your evidence, or your evidence will be that you left the hospital in due course. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise. I left the hospital, I went out through the entrance to the area called the emergency ward, and it was in that area that I met this civilian for whom they said that he was a criminal in disguise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Disguise. The -- I'd like to, if I may, please, deal with -- you've told us about the hospital, and I think it's right that you eventually left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left the hospital. I can't be fully accurate in telling you the time, but I left the hospital then, when I approached Lieutenant-Colonel Dr. Ivezic and the representative of the International Red Cross. It could have been after 10.30, closer to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Where did you then go to, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made an arrangement with Warrant Officer Korica to meet in the office of Captain Borisavljevic at Velepromet. I said this to Major Sljivancanin, telling him that I had accomplished my mission, touring the hospital and all, and that since I had seen a civilian there in an all-terrain vehicle, I believe it was a Land Rover, with Novi Sad licence plates, I asked him whether he could approach that civilian and ask him to take me to the command post of Velepromet, if this was where he was going anyway. Major Sljivancanin most likely spoke to this man. I don't know to this day who this man was, and he took me in his vehicle and drove me to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I know it's slightly earlier than we

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's slightly earlier than we would normally rise. But I'm coming on to a specific area that I would prefer to be given in one piece of evidence. And I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- ask for that to be done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will now adjourn for the first break. And I think it would be an opportune time to relax for a little bit and so we will adjourn until a quarter to 11.00 and resume then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, before the break you told us that you were then going -- after the hospital, you were going to go to Velepromet. So I'd like to deal now, please, with your return to the Velepromet area. Can you tell us approximately when it was you returned to the Velepromet area or facility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previously given statements, the ones I gave to the military judge, and then the one I gave to the Prosecutor, and also at the trial in the special court in Belgrade, it is clear that I was unable to pin-point the exact time. However, following my story I came to realise that I arrived there after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Velepromet, did you meet anyone?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman who drove me to Velepromet went on to the command post, as far as I could gather. There at the gate I found a military policeman who was guarding the facility; he was subordinated to Captain Borisavljevic. I asked him whether Warrant Officer Korica was there and he took me to the office, which Korica described as Captain Borisavljevic's office. There I found another captain, or perhaps captain first class, wearing the same kind of uniform that I wore. He was on duty by the phone, which was on a table, and he had on him an automatic weapon, a sub-machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was that -- what was that officer doing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that he was from the TO staff. That was my impression. Perhaps he was from the brigade of Colonel Mrksic, but I don't know this. Even though he and I introduced each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember his name? If you can't, do say so, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, truly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was Branko Korica doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Korica sat behind a desk, which was a low-type desk. And there was a brief-case on this desk, which had a numeric code. The brief-case was open, and he was already entering something into his notebook. He was writing something in it. I was surprised when I saw him take out some blue envelopes, put them on the desk, and emptied them of their contents, which were German marks, Deutschemarks, in -- and there was some other papers there, and he said that it came from the brief-case or belonged to the brief-case. And this is what he told me about the brief-case. He said that the military policeman at the reception desk, in the presence of Captain Borisavljevic, because when he came there from the hospital he found Captain Borisavljevic there. And apparently he handed over this brief-case saying, "Warrant officer, sir, the Chetniks gave this to me saying that I was to give you this personally." Korica felt uncomfortable and he used a local expression describing that, based on which I understood that he saw this as something that was embarrassing for him. In the brief-case there was a passport, a wallet, a passport with information about its holder. There was an empty wallet with a personal ID issued in the same name as the passport. As far as I remember, there was a cheque-book there with cheques of the Vukovar bank. Several cheques were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person whose cheque-book that -- who owned these cheque-books?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vladimir Vodopija. I remember the name because this problem remained with me. It stayed with me throughout my work at the KP Dom or penitentiary institution in Sremska Mitrovica. There was a stamp there as well, as well as the name of the company whose director, Vladimir Vodopija was. He was the director of the city water utility company of Vukovar. It was clear, based on those envelopes and what was written on them, that they were intended for his employees or from the members of the Vukovar TO, or perhaps members of some ZNG unit or volunteers who performed certain tasks in the war. These envelopes had money in them, between 15 to 18 marks, German marks, and it seems as though this money was for per diems. And there was also a stamp there enabling someone to withdraw money from the Vukovar bank, and then there was a cheque-book, based on which we concluded that the money was missing and that if there was a large sum of money belonging to this company or to the director and if that money came from the safe, we concluded that the money was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Whilst you were in the room at this time, were you informed of the arrival of any other people?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time the military policeman from the reception gate burst into the room. He was afraid. He opened the door of our room and said, visibly excited, "Arkan is here. Arkan came here to the compound with some civilians." Or perhaps he said "with some persons." We looked around, we were taken aback. My impression was, and I will describe it to you now what it was. I was surprised. Arkan normally doesn't go anywhere for no reason at all. He normally goes someplace when he has a very specific task. I concluded that he had come there with a specific task and that we were in for an unpleasant surprise, because wherever Arkan went, bad things happened. This is why I was surprised. I was wondering how come he came there on his own. I thought about Colonel Mrksic, Major Sljivancanin and myself. I wondered about the prisoners of war who had been already evacuated, as well as the events at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did any other person speak to you in relation to the arrival of Arkan after this soldier had told you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First a colonel came in and introduced himself. He was carrying a Heckler gun across his chest. A Heckler & Koch; that is a make. He asked who the most senior officer in the room was. I said my name was Colonel Branko. This is something I haven't shared with this Court so far, but I did say this at the special court in Belgrade while testifying. Why did I have this code-name, Colonel Branko? I can explain that right now, if you want me to, or perhaps later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal Colonel Branko at this time, if I may, as someone the Court may not be aware. When had you -- or why did you use the name Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules and principles governing the work of security bodies on special missions comprise special code-names being assigned to officers on a mission in order to protect their nearest and dearest from any unpleasant consequences that might arise from their activities. I selected a code-name for myself which I used when communicating with people I did not know. All those who were working closely with me knew my real name. I realised that I had been quite justified on several different occasions in using a code-name. It was a good thing for me to have one. The same applies to this incident involving Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Everybody called him Arkan. Jastreb, the commander of Vukovar's defence, also assumed a code-name. The other one, Mali [as interpreted] Jastreb, had also had a code-name, so that's the explanation I can offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can we deal then, please, with you saying to the colonel that your name was Colonel Branko. What did he reply, or did he reply, to you when you told them that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said immediately that Commander Arkan had arrived. I asked, "Which Commander Arkan do you mean?" There was an altercation between us, perhaps not so much as an altercation, but we were trying to outwit each other. It was a verbal duel. He was suggesting that Arkan should be perceived by me as some sort of authority, that I should go and meet Arkan in order to report to him. That was my understanding of the man's words. And I immediately concocted a plan in my head in a bid to protect both myself and all those present there. The important thing was to find out why Arkan was there to begin with. I suppose you're about to ask me other questions about this, and I will do my best to shed light on the issue and what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You're quite right. I am going to ask you some other questions. So what did you say to this -- this colonel after this disagreement with him? Can you paint a picture for the Court what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he tried to apply pressure for me to go and see Arkan, he tried to put me under pressure, but I refused. I said, "Colonel, if indeed you are a JNA colonel, then you must surely be aware of the rules and regulations that prevail. When you arrive in a barracks your duty is to report to a senior officer or a commanding officer. Doesn't it strike you as strange that I should now go and report to this man called Arkan? I don't know him and I don't know you. I don't know who you are." And then he started querying this by saying things like, "How come I didn't know Arkan, the commander of the Serb guards volunteers." He's famous throughout Europe and the world and I appeared to be the only person who never heard of him. He said he knew some of the officers from the security administration but that he had never heard my name in the context, whereupon I replied that I had never heard of him either. I did drop a couple of names of the officers from the Osijek garrison of the security administration. He had previously claimed that he worked there in one of the security bodies of the TO staff. When Tudjman's Ustashas entered Osijek, he lost his flat and he lost his family, after which he decided to join Arkan and he stayed close to him throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know if I asked you this question. My apologies if I have and I'm repeating myself. Do you know the name of this colonel, the colonel who came in and asked you to go and see Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can give you his last name. At first he introduced himself as Starcevic or Strikovic. There is another last name I had in mind which now escapes me. I don't believe that I am able to give you his last name though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. After this discussion with this colonel, did he remain with you or did he leave?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left. Every time he left, he left in order to bring Arkan up to speed on the state of our altercation. Arkan was gradually finding out about my position and my answers. So we were locked in a game of trying to verbally outwit each other, both biding our time to see what would happen. I am about to describe this for you, and I already spoke about this in one of my statements. At one point in time, Arkan appeared at the door carrying a Heckler gun across his chest. His right fist was bandaged, and he was wearing a number of -- he was wearing a sling across his shoulder. He looked at us in order to survey the scene and then he spoke to me. He said, "Colonel, you are a foolhardy man. You must be both mad and silly. Where do you get the courage to take 2.000 Ustasha war criminals away from here? Where did you take them to, and you will have to bring them back from wherever it was that you had taken them to."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When he said that to you, did you reply?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said, "And how about you, clever man, where do you get the courage to know exactly how many were there? How on earth do you know that there were 2.000 of them, and how on earth do you know that they were all criminals of war?" I said a number of other things along the same lines, looking him in the eyes all the while trying to fathom what his real intentions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you replied in this way to him, did he -- did he reply to your challenge?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He started explaining by saying that all those people were Ustashas and criminals. I kept replying that there weren't 2.000 of them to begin with, that we had only taken away as many as 800. I reiterated that I was Colonel Branko from the security administration and that I was there along with a team with a specific mission, a mission imparted to us by the chief of the security administration. I said that those people were prisoners of war. I clearly explained that to him in no uncertain terms. We had a discussion about the fact that there may well have been Ustashas and criminals among those people for as long as they were firing at his fighters and guards members, as he called them. But from the moment they surrendered, hands up in the air and lay down their arms, they became prisoners of war. I also explained that they had been evacuated to the Sremska Mitrovica correctional facility, and that they would be screened there by the security bodies and it -- if necessary, prosecuted by the judicial authorities. I said I had no doubt that the criminals among them would be found out. I told him that it was a long and demanding process by which if you vetted people for war crimes, I said it would require some degree of cooperation with the local population in order to find out which of those people had committed any crimes, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about this, what I will use the word "confrontation." Did the hostile environment remain with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The tone remained hostile until the point in time when I told him that we had been acting according to the law and under the rules of the international law of war and in keeping with them throughout, and that it was quite obvious to me that he knew nothing about those rules, but that regardless of that these rules had to be observed. He again pattered on about how those people were criminals and that they had been killing the Serbian people. He knew it for a fact, he said, that those people were criminals, because many of his own fighters of his own guards members had been killed and that I had no idea about how many of his -- of his people had been killed in their struggle for the freedom of the Serbian people, in addition to which he kept saying that both he personally and his guards members were fighting for the benefit of the Serbs, Serbs living anywhere between Canada and Australia. And that he made an enormous contribution to that cause. This may not be the exact sequence of our exchange, but I believe I have told you about all the substantial topics that were raised during our confrontation. Apart from this, he also tried to convince me that the JNA security bodies were doing a lousy work in protecting the Serbian people and that they were doing nothing to track down war criminals. It was in this context that he referred to a lady he called Magda. Based on his information, he said she had slit the throats of as many as 40 young children. He said he was in the process of informing the relevant JNA security bodies about this incident, and I assured him that this would be thoroughly checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Arkan himself indicate to you what he thought or how you thought prisoners of wars should be treated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he and members of his guards recognised no such thing as prisoners of war. Recognised no such thing as surrender or people surrendering. He said that all those who had been killing the Serb people were war criminals in his eyes, or mere criminals. I said, "What do you mean, Arkan? What do you mean you don't recognise prisoners of war, given the fact that you yourself were captured at one point?" His facial expression suddenly changed. This was something that he had a bit of a reputation for, you might say. He had the skills of an actor, you might say, in changing the expressions of his face. He faced me across the table and said, "It is true that I was at one point captured. I was held in a prison in Zagreb. You seem to know about this. It was thanks to divine intervention, providence or whatever you want to call that, that I survived." I said, "Arkan, all that actually happened was you were exchanged as part of a regular procedure controlled by the government." He just glossed over this and started going on again about his contribution, the contribution that he made, as well as the members of his guards unit, about how he helped the generals and young JNA soldiers with next to no experience to survive and take them back to their mothers and families, as he said. I told him that no doubt the Serbian people would give credit where credit was due, and that the mothers would as well, but that there was still no need to commit any further crimes. We went on talking about crimes happening on both sides, in both camps, as it were. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. You're talking about a discussion with Arkan about crimes by both parties. Did he indicate to you what he thought would occur if you killed one group of people or if the Croats killed a number of Serbs? Did he have any particular philosophy in relation to that, what I will call tit-for-tat killing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose his understanding of the issue could be described as tit for tat. He said there was no such thing in his eyes as taking prisoners or prisoners, and that applied to his men too. All those who had been killing people were to be killed themselves. That was what he said. Even that menacing sentence that he addressed me with when he first came implied as much. He knew what had occurred at Velepromet. At least that was the impression I had. In addition to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, "In addition to this"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say he kept talking about the contribution that he had made, as well as his men, about how he had helped the generals. He pulled out a photograph to show me, showing him hugging a general of the Novi Sad Corps, Andrija Biorcevic. I meant no harm at the time, but I told him that I knew something about this sort of thing too. I asked him, "Do you have a photograph hugging the previous commander of the Novi Sad Corps, General Radic, who lay down his life for peace, in order to have peace in the Vukovar area, to restore peace?" He lay down his life for this objective. He gave all that he had to give." I told Arkan I knew General Andrija Biorcevic because we were schoolmates at the higher military school I also knew Mladin Bratic, I said, because we were schoolmates from the officer's school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There came a time clearly when Arkan left; is that right? Left the room certainly.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a colonel accompanying him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was about to say. And who was the next person you had dealings with?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this colonel who was escorting him who came in and said that he was wanted and needed elsewhere. He left in a hurry. I stayed back in the office, and I was making a draft for a report that I would later be submitting. I had this discussion with Warrant Officer Korica. We were trying to arrive at some sort of conclusion as to why Arkan had come there. After a while, this colonel named Strikovic or Starcevic, whatever, came in and said, "Colonel Branko is wanted at the government meeting of the SAO Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem." He may not have used these very words, but he was clear about one thing: I was wanted at the SAO government meeting. That much was clear. I was stunned by this. What government was he talking about? What meeting at Velepromet was he talking about? Why Velepromet of all places? It was then that it suddenly dawned on me that Arkan was not there for nothing. It dawned on me that things would start happening which only bode ill, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you go to this so-called government?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The message was delivered to me in a sharp voice. I settled down the corridor, and through the glass pane I saw quite a number of persons standing there, some of them wearing uniform, some wearing the MUP uniform, the police uniform. I told Branko Korica to get that brief-case and to follow me as fast as he could as well as to try to follow what was going on around us. I came to the room where I had held that officer's meeting the previous night. You asked me about the meeting, and I described to you what the meeting was about, when we were trying to empty those rooms in Velepromet and evacuate the POWs. It was in this same room, it was a rather large office, in fact, that the government meeting was held which I attended in a way, which I am about to describe. The tables were arranged in a square, you might say. There were several tables at the back, to the left. I was facing the door on my way in. There was a rather long table too. There was Ilija -- I can't remember the person's last name. I should go back to my statement to check. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. We'll leave that just for the moment. Did you recognise any politicians there at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Goran Hadzic, prime minister, was there. His face was familiar from photographs, from the printed press. I knew that he was the prime minister. He came in, we exchanged greetings. He sat down beside Mr. Ilija, who was the president of the Assembly of the Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem SAO. And then ministers started appearing in the room. Seated at the same table, facing both them and me, was the justice minister, Mr. Vojin Susa. I understood the person seated next to him to be the late Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just stop you for a moment? You use the title Goran Hadzic, prime minister. Who gave him the title of prime minister? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gleaned from what I was told, and I was being told that I was showing no respect for the generals and for the government, and I gleaned from the context that the government had been elected by the people and that was where they derived their legitimacy from. It was made clear to me that this was something that I had to show respect for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why do you say you were being accused of not showing respect to this so-called government?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back to the original sequence as given in my statement. By your leave, I would like to tackle one thing at a time in order to shed light on what exactly happened there. The prime minister Goran Hadzic opened the meeting. I can tell you what he talked about, what the meeting was about. I can tell you about my own experience at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like, if you could, in a shortened form, to tell us what the meeting apparently was about, and if there is any areas that I wish to ask more questions about, or my learned friends wish to ask any more questions, we will do so. But if you could try and keep your answer fairly short in this area.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly Goran Hadzic opened the meeting the following way: He said, "I am opening the meeting of our government with the same agenda as the one we had for the previous meeting." This already gave me the impression that I either was not supposed to learn what the agenda of the meeting was or that I was going to find out during the meeting itself. In the statement where I described the meeting, I forgot to mention that there was another -- or a second item on the agenda, because the prosecutor at the special court asked me what the second item was, and I thought about it for a while and told the prosecutor the following: He stated at the meeting that this was the continuation of a meeting that had been held at some point earlier somewhere. The first one who asked for the floor was Minister of Justice, Vojin Susa, and he asked Goran to be allowed to put some questions to the colonel in order for the colonel to answer these questions in front of everyone. The questions included the following: Where was I going on -- where did I, and on whose orders and why take 1.500 Ustashas and criminals who had been killing the Serbian people. And I followed the same sequence in answering these questions. I told them that I was a member of the team from the security administration headed by Slavko Tomic, that we were there on a mission given by the chief of the security administration, I said this was General such and such, and that we were there to assist Colonel Mrksic's unit in evacuating prisoners of war from the combat area. I also said that what we were doing was within the scope of law. His question to me was whose prisoners of war were they? I answered that they were prisoners of the state. His question was, who captured them? I answered that they had been captured by fighters in the area of responsibility of Colonel Mrksic's brigade; therefore, they were captured by JNA and TO units. I also explained why they had been taken to the correctional facility at Sremska Mitrovica, that their POW camp had been set up there accordance with the regulations. His question to me was, who was going interrogate these people and further bring them to justice? I said that there were both investigators and military prosecutors there who were going to deal with this. His question was, pursuant to which laws was this procedure to be conducted under. My answer was that this was going to be under the federal laws, since the correctional facility at Sremska Mitrovica was a federal facility and that was the reason why they had been taken there in the first place. That this was to be done and was done with the approval of at least two federal ministries and of the top military leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about the definition of "war criminal," who was a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in such a position that I had to explain that they may as well have been Ustashas and war criminals. However, I emphasised that this was the case until the moment they surrendered, raised their hands, and laid their weapons. From that moment on, they became prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: During this meeting were there any other officers present? When I say "officers" I mean either TO or JNA.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 30 people there. I don't think all of them were ministers, which means that there were assistant to the ministers there, that there was the chief of the SUP, I don't know what his name was, there was his assistant there as well. Furthermore, there was Ljuban Devetak wearing a uniform. He was the commander of some TO staff and of some TO unit. He also took part in the discussion and displayed hostility toward the Yugoslav People's Army and toward myself. He uttered the following words, "The JNA had destroyed and wrecked Vukovar. The JNA made a new Stalingrad out of Vukovar. This will be the sort of history that the Croatian children will be taught and they will be indoctrinated." He used very strong language also toward the JNA generals, and there were some things to that effect that were addressed to me, I believe, by the late Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask about your personal safety? Did you at any time feel that your personal safety was at risk?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. During the meeting at least three persons used very strong language and threats to me. Whereas Arkan, who had the sort of facial expression he can -- could normally be seen with, waited and listened to all of this and waited to hear what the government was going to -- what sort of position it was going to take in relation to my person and my life. I felt a hostage there, and I say so openly before this Trial Chamber and the Tribunal that I respect. I want to clearly state that I was a hostage at this government meeting. I seem to remember that Slavko Dokmanovic suggested at some point and the -- and he addressed the suggestion to Goran Hadzic that we decide what to do with Vukovar. He --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, what to do with colonel.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he should be asked to bring those POWs back from Sremska Mitrovica, where he had taken them. And I said, "Well, how -- what do you mean? They were taken over there in an organised fashion, and this is exactly the manner in which they should be taken back." However, he merely ignored what I said and insisted on his idea. Goran Hadzic was following this in silence without reacting, and there was one man next to the door whom he addressed - he was a minister - and told him, "Please take a look to see whether there is a lieutenant-colonel, whether he arrived." This minister who was seated next to the door said on several occasions that the lieutenant-colonel had not yet arrived. I didn't know who this lieutenant-colonel was who they were mentioning. And -- and then I was told, well, the persons in attendance were told that, "Well, somebody else should join the colonel here so that he does not feel on his own as a JNA officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was this the first time that you had become aware that there was a lieutenant-colonel involved in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt that this was just a pretext that they were using, although I allowed for a possibility that there was somebody else there who had been given a mission and was supposed to come back from that mission. As far as I remember, Mr. Goran Hadzic told the minister who was seated next to the door to check whether the man had come back two or three times, and I believe it was actually three times that they went out into the corridor to check if the lieutenant-colonel had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, you used the phrase "the man" and then went on to say "to check if the lieutenant-colonel had come." Did a lieutenant-colonel come eventually?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they had levelled threats and exerted pressure against me, Slavko Dokmanovic told me, "What sort of state are you referring to, Colonel? Yugoslavia, you can see that it is no more. What sort of JNA are you referring to? Don't you see that it is gone? What is left of the JNA is being commanded over by generals who are not Serbs. Don't you see that these generals don't like Serbs anyway?" In that context, he mentioned the topmost generals, the top-ranking generals, Veljko Kadijevic -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. You've told us that on three occasions people had gone to see if a lieutenant-colonel had returned or had come. Now, I'd like to deal with that topic, please. Do you understand the topic? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll just follow that through. So did a lieutenant-colonel come or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reiterate this sentence. After the strongest of pressure had been exerted on me, along the lines of, very well, those POWs who had been evacuated had been evacuated. However, we would not be allowed to take those men hiding in the hospital, those criminals out of the hospital further than the barracks, that the barracks was already encircled by members of the TO Vukovar and the civilian population. That, if need be, more of the ordinary people, population, would be brought in to physically prevent the buses from leaving by lying across the road. They added further threats against my person to me. Then I told them, "These are not prisoners of war. I told you these are not my prisoners of war. I told you where they were." At that point, we heard a knock on the door while Goran was addressing the meeting, and Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, Chief of Staff of Colonel Mrksic entered, holding a notebook or some sort of folder in his arms. Goran Hadzic had seen him immediately stood up and all the ministers who were next to the door surrounded Panic and all of them together left the room with Lieutenant-Colonel Panic without paying any attention to me, as if I had not been there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether there was any conversation, not hear, were you able to see if there where is any conversation between Panic and the group of people around?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had a sort of conversation, and I was only able to see that gestures, facial expressions, and I saw them leave the room in a hurry. However, I don't know the contents of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question. Did they ever tell you what the conversation was about? When you say that you saw them leave the room in a hurry, do you know where they went?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. But as there was mention of buses, evacuation of the hospital, criminals who would not be allowed to be evacuated, and there was mention of all possible measures to be taken without, of course, asking them, I concluded that Susa -- based on what Susa had said that they were ready to set up a court-martial, he said that they had very experienced prosecutors and judges, and they were perfectly able to function within the remit of the law as any other prosecutorial body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Please wait for a moment. Now, when you were told by Susa that they would be able to cope, the phrase that you use was "able to function within the remit of the law," did you believe at that time that they had the structure for trying prisoner of wars? Did you say anything to them or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
