utterances.text: I expressed my objection to that and asked them whether they had the necessary conditions and human resources to embark on such an enterprise, and that probably the JNA leadership was not going to be opposed to that, but that they would nevertheless like to give their consent. And I told them that I myself was not authorised to give them the consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you leave the building where the meeting had taken place?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not leave the building immediately. I will tell the truth before this Trial Chamber in saying that I feared for my life. I therefore waited for a while and proceeded to the office where I had left Korica behind. I could not find him there, so I took my back-pack and my belongings, and as I was leaving the room - I was still on the premises - I saw two cameramen. I don't know whether they belonged to a TV crew. But there was a journalist who I knew from before, he was Mr. Peternek. I had seen some of his work before. I hurried toward the exit of the building, and I saw a person wearing a military sort of hat, and he yelled out, "Look at him, another Commie is passing by. Let's get hold of him."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time go to the JNA barrack area after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I rushed straight to the barracks to seek protection there, because I anticipated more threats and danger from those quarters. I omitted to say that as soon as I returned from the hospital Korica told me that a lieutenant sniper shooter told him, "You should feel lucky because they had warned me that were you not the Colonel Branko, but another different Branko." I then arrived at the barracks -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. When you arrived at the barracks, did you see any buses there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no buses at the barracks. I didn't see any. There were some frozen puddles on the ground that I crossed on my way to the barracks, where I approached a guard, asking him to take me to the commander to report to him. He took me to the commander, and I was surprised to see the face that I knew from before, and that was the face of Major Lukic, who I knew very well. We served at the Pancevo barracks together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any civilians at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any civilians, but after I had had lunch - we had the beans for lunch - I told the major that I had not eaten in 24 hours, we chatted a bit and then as I was going down the corridor I heard a woman coughing. I asked her who that was, and the guard who was there told me that Dr. Bosanac was there along with some other people. I came to the conclusion that they were brought there to be held there as in a military detention, because every barracks had its military detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have mentioned a Dr. Bosanac being there. Were any other names given to you who were being detained at that time with Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I arrived at my conclusion based on what Major Sljivancanin had explained, that he had been talking to Dr. Bosanac, Dr. Njavro, and Marin Vidic, Bili. And that was how I arrived at the conclusion that they were held in detention there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever return to Negoslavci, the command centre in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I went back there. But before that I met Colonel Milan Gvero at the barracks. He was assistant to the chief for information, or perhaps he himself was the chief for public information in the secretariat for national defence. Colonel Milan Gvero told me that he was drafting a press release for the public, both in the country and worldwide, because -- because they -- the journalists were supposed to visit Vukovar on the 21st of November. I also saw Rade Leskovac, a minister in Goran Hadzic's government. He put provocative questions to me by saying, "What would you say, Colonel, in percentages, to what extent has Vukovar been destroyed?" I -- destroyed by the JNA, that is. And I returned him in the same measure, although I don't remember how it was that I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, I am just asking to stop for a moment because sometimes you speak very quickly and it's difficult for the interpreters. Now, let's deal, if we may, please, about your return to the command centre at Negoslavci. So can we deal with that topic, please? When did you return to the command centre at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my recollection, that was at about 1800 hours. It was dark. I found Colonel Kijanovic there, Colonel Tomic, and there were some other persons there as well, in front of the command headquarters. Then they briefed me, saying that the buses had been taken from the barracks to Ovcara. Kijanovic said that he took out four JNA soldiers from the bus. They were prisoners of war of the Croatian army and they had also been wounded and hospitalised. I was supposed to explain to you that when touring the hospital I explicitly requested for Dr. Stanojevic to take me to the area or to the room where these soldiers were. If you need me to elaborate on this, I can do this. I believe it to be relevant. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm quite sure there will be questions about that, but can we just please remain on the return to the command centre at Negoslavci? You've told us about Kijanovic being there and Tomic being there and you'd had heard that the buses had gone to Ovcara. Well, may I just ask the question? Thank you. With regard to the buses, had all the buses gone to Ovcara, as far as you are aware, or not? And if you can't remember, do say so.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't say all buses. They just referred to those carrying criminals of war. We know that there were medical staff members at the hospitals, doctors, civilians and so on. And that there were these people in disguise. They simply said that only buses carrying these persons, whom they referred to as Ustashas and war criminals, had departed, and Kijanovic said that from one such bus he had taken out JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about Tomic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Slavko Tomic said that he went because of that two or three times to see Colonel Mrksic to intervene in relation to these buses and that he managed to reach Colonel Mrksic. He said that at that time there was another colonel there wearing the air force uniform. He said that he warned him about the fact that the TO members wanted to take buses to Ovcara by using force. As far as I remember, he said that Colonel Mrksic was silent, but that he raised his hand and put it in front of his eyes, based on which he concluded that the TO members should be -- basically that they should turn a blind eye in relation to the actions of TO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me for one moment, please? I just want to check something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with Kijanovic at this time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to Kijanovic about what was going on there, how it was going to end. I related my experiences to them about the government cabinet session. I said that Arkan was there, and I briefly conveyed to them the substance that can also be found in my statement and in my evidence here before this Trial Chamber. I said that pressure had been exerted on me a number of times, threats were issued. I couldn't say that I survived by chance, but rather that I survived, thanks to the JNA members who were implementing their tasks, and those were members subordinated to Colonel Mrksic and to Sljivancanin, which means that I would not have been able to accomplish my task had they not helped me. Kijanovic told me that he had taken measures and steps, as we say in our parlance, and approached either Colonel Mrksic or some other senior officer and was given military policemen and a truck. Then they toward the Velepromet compound -- my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do carry on.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then he said that he had found 17 corpses, that they transported them to the military graveyard and buried. I thanked him, because he had promised to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal then, please, in, I hope, brief, in a brief way, did you eventually leave the Negoslavci command centre and return towards Sid?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We waited for a long time for a column to be formed and for them to depart to Sid. As far as I was concerned, I don't know what happened afterwards. However, we waited there for a long time, long into the night, perhaps it was close to 2300 hours or midnight. Our vehicle was at the helm of a long column, including an armoured personnel carrier, and when the decision was made for the column to move, we set out towards Sid. I said this in my statement, and I must repeat it before this Trial Chamber as well. Namely, at that time one could hear bursts of fire, fire to the left of us, and this sounded ominous. There perhaps were some comments to that effect. In one of my statements I mentioned these comments, and it was interpreted as though I was advocating a group opinion. And then I said that what was written in the statement was not true and that I could have kept my opinion to myself without expressing it to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to the gun-fire, are you able to indicate to the Court -- you've said to the left, which of course depends really which way you're standing. But if one considers the various towns or locations, and you are in Negoslavci, are you able to say in which direction the gun-fire came from? And if you aren't, please say so. Don't guess.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a topographic map on me, which I had brought with me from Belgrade. I also had rules on the application of the international law. I brought this material with me from Belgrade. As an officer when one arrives in a certain area, one has to orient oneself and then find reference points, settlements, and so on. Many times at meetings I heard Ovcara being mentioned -- rather, cabinet ministers mentioned it, including others who were there, brigade members and so on. It was mentioned by Slavko Tomic and Kijanovic as well. I might have even asked them in what direction it was, and they said that it was approximately in the same general area where we were all lined up, and this is how I concluded that this -- these bursts of fire had come from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And which area is that, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the direction of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, please, with your arrival at Sid? Did you report to any senior officer there after you had left Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The column travelled for a long time. Pursuant to the orders of Colonel Tomic, we halted in front of the command post of Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic, which was in the office of the -- in the premises of the main post office in Sid. And the column continued on to Mitrovica or to Belgrade, or I didn't know exactly where. We entered the premises of Colonel Petkovic's command post and there, at the entrance, in one of the rooms we were first met by General Mile Babic. He, in the security chain of command, was superior to Colonel Petkovic, chief of security of the 1st Military District; that was his post. He was present there, he greeted us, we spent a brief time talking to him there. Colonel Tomic went to the office where Colonel Petkovic was, and they would spend quite a lot of time there together. Some officers would come out from that room; they were not familiar to me. I remember that I also saw a lady who might have been a journalist or something, but she was in a uniform. Also, Captain Petkovic came to greet me, Kijanovic, and the rest who were there from our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I heard Captain Petkovic. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Petkovic. Unless I misspoke, which means that I might be tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you're tired, perhaps we're all rather tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder if Your Honour might consider it to be an appropriate moment and I then should conclude in the following period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now, Mr. Moore. And in the circumstances, perhaps half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I deal with one preliminary matter? The Colonel has spoken to the witness assistance person and indicated that he's feeling very tired, having given evidence now for two days and obviously been here in The Hague. I anticipate that I would have 10 or 15 minutes to take up by way of examination-in-chief. What I would respectfully ask the Court to consider would be for me to conclude my examination-in-chief and for the evidence to stop there this afternoon and to resume on Monday with what I will call clean start on cross-examination from Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, would it help you to organise your thoughts over the weekend? Further organise them. Don't think that I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you kindly, Your Honour. The Defence is prepared to do that. However, in the -- or rather, in the similar cases when we have done so in the past, it always produced positive results. We have always shown nothing but understanding for the needs of the witness and the OTP. So we have no objections in this case either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am encouraged, Mr. Vasic, but the Chamber is aware that we have noticed that at times counsel have been extremely responsive to suggestions that time should be watched and matters concentrated. So we hope that the advantage of having a full weekend to prepare for that will assist all cross-examining counsel. Thank you for your cooperation. Yes, Mr. Moore, we will break after your evidence in chief has concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, may we just resume, please, where we left off before the adjournment. You had told us about reporting to Sid where you saw Colonel Petkovic and General Babic. Now, I would like to deal, please, with that particular meeting or those meetings. Did you at any time inform either Babic or Petkovic what you had seen and witnessed at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my experience so far, whenever there were complex problems or issues I would do this, and so I asked General Babic whether he was aware of what was going on in the area of responsibility or area of operations of Colonel Mrksic. And in relation to the task that we were working on, he said that he was aware of everything. I did not explain anything further, nor did I ask anything after that. We stayed there waiting for Colonel Petkovic to come and greet us. Then I asked him, too, in the presence of General Babic and other officers, whether he was aware of what had happened there, what was going on there, and what we had experienced. He said too that he was aware of everything. Colonel Slavko Tomic had already been to see him in his office. I don't know who else might have been there in that office. As I have already told you, I saw a lady, a lady wearing a military uniform who had come out of his office. I've seen that before. We stayed there for quite a long time. They offered us coffee and cognac. And this is where we stayed until it was time for us to go to Sremska Mitrovica. As for the column which travelled behind us, I don't know where it went afterwards. I also don't know who was in the APC either. I can say that when conducting interviews within the scope of my authorities, when talking to Dr. Vesna Bosanac and Dr. Bilus, I had heard from them that previously in that APC they were taken first to Belgrade and then returned back to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I deal now with your position in relation to giving evidence before this Tribunal? It is right, is it not, that you did not wish to give evidence before this Tribunal unless there was an official request served on you through the normal administrative channels. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first notice to come and be interviewed by The Hague investigators is something that I understood as my duty. In addition to that, as a former member of the JNA, as a former member of the security organ, I realised that I needed to have an authorisation from some kind of a government institution, be it an army or another state institution or some minister perhaps. Based on that, I drafted an application and tried to file it with the Ministry of Defence, to submit it there in the building called Kula, in Knez Milos Street, right next to the building where I used to work, which was destroyed by NATO bombs. I waited for a long time at the reception desk to be told whether somebody would see me. They always denied my request with the explanation that the defence minister was not present. I was persistent, however. I pressed on because I wanted somebody to meet with me. I wanted to be sure that there would be no adverse consequences for me later on. I met with chef de cabinet of Colonel Karanfilov. As far as I can remember, he was a member of the security organ in Vukovar as well, subordinated to Major Sljivancanin. He certainly was not in the position to make a decision himself. Refused my request to meet with the assistance -- assistant or deputy defence minister. I heard when one of his superiors asked him whether he knew me, and I was in the vicinity, and he must have not heard about me earlier because he said that he hadn't met me in Vukovar. The colonel that I spoke to, I told him that it was their duty to give me an authorisation to go and meet with The Hague investigators. At that point in time, the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal had not yet been passed. Fortunately, it was passed a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into a it in any more detail. And as a direct consequence of various formal documentation, you now attend before The Hague to give this evidence. Is that right? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. I must explain this. The last time I was summoned by this Tribunal I again requested in writing a formal request by the Tribunal for me to appear before the Court and testify. I addressed the National Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, the National Council of Serbia and Montenegro. I asked to be received. I obtained certain documents from them. The first time I went to talk to you, documents were handed over to me at the Belgrade MUP central office. It is for this reason that I have a number of documents with me. There is a document dated 2000 that I was not free to disclose any state or military secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you have been advised of that. But if I may put it in the round, you have come to give evidence in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a phone call from Mr. van -- can you help me along with this, please, van Rooyen or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: He is an investigator called Mr. van Rooyen. Can I just deal with it in this way? Perhaps it's the easiest way and we can finish you giving your evidence. That you did eventually receive a telephone call from an investigator here, the Office of the Prosecutor, and as a direct consequence of that, arrangements were made for you to attend?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, as indicated, we propose now to adjourn for today, resuming on Monday at 2.15. So that you will have a rest period over the weekend, sir, and we will continue your evidence on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
